title: Leadership
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The essay presents a framework for one of leadership's most consequential micro-decisions: when a team member is struggling, a leader must choose between high support (emotional, relational, presence-based) and low support (directive, analytical, problem-solving). The wrong choice, giving analytical advice to someone who needs emotional acknowledgment or providing comfort when someone urgently needs direction, is not just unhelpful but actively damages the leader-member relationship. The author's central insight is that leaders tend to default to the support style reflecting their own preference or strength, not what the team member actually needs. Effective leaders learn to read the situation before choosing, which requires suppressing the instinctive support style long enough to notice what the team member is actually asking for. The essay treats this matching skill as learnable and improvable through attention and deliberate practice.
points: High support (emotional presence, acknowledgment, relational investment) and low support (directive coaching, problem-solving, concrete guidance) are not better or worse in absolute terms; each is right in specific circumstances and wrong in others.

Leaders systematically mis-calibrate support type because they default to the modality they find most comfortable or natural, rather than reading what the struggling team member actually needs in the moment.

Providing analytical advice to someone who needs emotional acknowledgment first is a common and damaging mismatch, signaling that the leader is not attending to what the team member is actually experiencing.
Reading which support mode is appropriate is learnable: listen for whether the team member is describing a feeling or a problem, and whether they are asking for help thinking or just for presence.

Leaders who develop fluency in both support modes and learn to defer their natural style in favor of what is needed build significantly stronger individual relationships and team resilience during difficulty.
quotes: Leaders are in the business of helping those who report to them. Whenever a team member hits a wall, leaders are there to lend a hand. The problem could be a stalled project, a skill gap, a failing relationship, or a situation too delicate to navigate alone.

How they help comes down to a deceptively simple choice: when offering support, leaders can "go high" or they can "go low." Going high means elevating the solution above both the leader and the team member. As the metaphor implies, the leader goes above the situation to survey the broader landscape, spots what is needed, and pulls it in.

Going low means the leader descends into the work alongside the team member. They pull up a chair, roll up their sleeves, and work through the problem together. Imagine a new sales rep who can't crack a difficult client conversation.

The leader sits on the next call, debriefs in real time, and coaches from inside the problem. Going high preserves the leader's time, builds the team member's network, and creates independence. Going low builds trust, transfers knowledge directly, and is often the only way to solve the problem quickly.

Go high too often, and you are likely a hands-off manager who only leads when called upon. Go low as a default, and you are likely a micro-manager who gets into the weeds on everything, and not just when asked. The wrong instinct is to always default to one or the other.

The right question isn't "Which approach is better?" It's "Which approach best fits the situation?" To make that call, leaders should consider three factors: urgency, capability gap, and growth stage. If this is a common problem that Page 1 others have faced, go high. If the team member is early in their development and needs attention, go low.
